summary: Describes how OSPFv3 can carry multiple address families by running multiple instances, mapping each family to an instance using the Instance ID field in the packet header. It is a proposed standard and needs few changes to OSPFv3.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5838 lets OSPFv3 carry routes for several address families by assigning each family to its own protocol instance. A new AF-bit helps routers identify peers that support the additional address families.

questions: what is the ospfv3 af bit
how does ospfv3 support multiple address families
subtitle: How OSPFv3 uses separate instances to carry routes for different address families.

tldr.problem: OSPFv3 was defined for IPv6 unicast, while networks also need to advertise IPv6 multicast, IPv4 unicast, and IPv4 multicast prefixes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps each address family to a range of OSPFv3 Instance IDs. Each Instance ID represents a separate instance with its own neighbors, link-state database, and shortest-path calculation; an AF-bit helps prevent incompatible routers from forming adjacencies in the new families.
tldr.outcome: The approach adds limited changes to OSPFv3 and allows gradual deployment. RFC 5838 has been updated by RFC 6969, RFC 7949, RFC 8362, and RFC 9454.

today: RFC 5838 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6969, RFC 7949, RFC 8362, and RFC 9454. It extends OSPFv3 as defined in RFC 5340.

sections.title: Why OSPFv3 Uses Multiple Instances
sections.content:
OSPFv3 was defined to support the base IPv6 unicast address family. RFC 5838 adds a way to support IPv6 multicast, IPv4 unicast, and IPv4 multicast by mapping each address family to a separate Instance ID and OSPFv3 instance.

The RFC chooses this approach because OSPFv3 already supports multiple instances. It keeps separate link-state databases for each family and minimizes changes to the protocol and to most existing configuration models.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPFv3 can keep separate routing instances, so this RFC assigns each address family to its own instance. Each instance maintains its own routing information and path calculation.

sections.title: Instance ID Ranges
sections.content:
The RFC assigns Instance ID ranges to address families. Values 0 to 31 are for IPv6 unicast, 32 to 63 for IPv6 multicast, 64 to 95 for IPv4 unicast, and 96 to 127 for IPv4 multicast. The first value in each range is the default for that family. Values 128 to 255 are unassigned.

Each Instance ID implies a separate OSPFv3 instance with its own neighbor adjacencies, link-state database, protocol data structures, and shortest-path-first computation. Prefixes that do not match the instance's address family MUST NOT be used in its route computation. OSPFv3 control packets still use IPv6, so IPv6 must be enabled on the link.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address family uses its own block of Instance ID values. The first value in a block is its default, and each selected value starts a separate routing instance.

sections.title: The AF-bit and Router Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC adds an AF-bit to the OSPFv3 Options field. A router supporting these address families MUST set the bit in Hello packets, Database Description packets, and Link State Advertisements. A router participating in an address family MUST discard Hello packets without the AF-bit, except in the base IPv6 unicast family, where the check MUST NOT be made for backward compatibility.

This check prevents a router that does not understand the extension from forming an adjacency in an instance reserved for another address family. IPv6 unicast behavior is unchanged, and the RFC says the other families can be deployed gradually without disturbing domains that include non-capable routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The AF-bit tells a router that its neighbor understands the additional address-family rules. For those families, routers reject Hello messages without the bit; IPv6 unicast keeps its compatibility exception.

sections.title: IPv4 Next Hops and Forwarding Addresses
sections.content:
For IPv4 unicast and multicast instances, the RFC places a link's IPv4 address in the first 32 bits of the IPv4 instance's Link-LSA link-local-address field. The remaining bits MUST be zero. This provides an IPv4 next-hop address for those families.

For IPv4 address families, the Forwarding Address in AS-external-LSAs and NSSA-LSAs also encodes an IPv4 address in its first 32 bits, with the remaining bits set to zero. Virtual links are not supported in address families other than IPv6 unicast because their control packets need a routable global IPv6 address.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 instances place an IPv4 address in the defined part of existing OSPFv3 fields to identify next hops and forwarding destinations. Virtual links remain limited to IPv6 unicast.

sections.title: MTU Checks for Other Address Families
sections.content:
For a non-IPv6 address family, routers must consider both that family's MTU and the IPv6 MTU used to determine the largest OSPFv3 packet. The Database Description packet's Interface MTU field carries the MTU for the advertised family, and a receiver rejects a packet whose MTU exceeds its interface MTU for that family.

The M6-bit indicates that the sender uses a different IPv6 MTU from the address-family MTU. If the bit is set, an optional IPv6 MTU TLV carries the IPv6 MTU; if the TLV is absent, the RFC says the IPv6 minimum of 1280 octets SHOULD be used for comparison.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers compare the packet size against the MTU for its address family. The M6-bit and optional IPv6 MTU TLV provide the separate IPv6 MTU when it differs.

sections.title: Security and Assigned Values
sections.content:
IPsec can provide OSPFv3 authentication and confidentiality. When multiple OSPFv3 instances use the same interface, they MUST use the same Security Association because the selectors cannot distinguish packets by fields such as Instance ID.

IANA assigned the AF-bit, M6-bit, and IPv6 MTU TLV type 17, and created an Instance ID address-family registry. This RFC assigns Instance IDs 0 to 127; assignment in the range 128 to 255 requires a Standards Track RFC with an IANA Considerations section.
sections.plainLanguage: Instances sharing an interface use the same security association because the security selectors do not distinguish their Instance IDs. The RFC also assigns values and sets a process for assigning the remaining Instance IDs.
